q: 1. The direction of shear stress is
explain: Unlike normal stress, shear stress acts tangential or parallel to the surface of the plane.

q: 2. The actual numerical value of tensile stress (engineering stress) is .............. than the theoretical stress
explain: Engineering stress is calculated using the original cross-sectional area, whereas theoretical (true) stress accounts for the reduction in area during tension.

q: 3. Allowable stress in steel is less than
explain: For safety, the allowable or working stress is always kept significantly lower than the yield stress of the material to prevent permanent deformation.

q: 4. The property by which a body returns to its original shape after removal of the force, is called
explain: Elasticity is defined as the property of a material to regain its original shape and size once the deforming force is removed.

q: 5. Elasticity of a body is defined
options: the property by which a body returns to its original shape after removal of load
the property by which a body don't returns to its original shape after removal of load
the property by which a body undergoes deformation even after removal of load
explain: Elasticity is the physical property that allows a material to return to its original dimensions after the unloading process.

q: 6. As the elastic limit reaches, tensile strain
options: increases in proportion to the stress
decreases in proportion to the stress
explain: Near the elastic limit, the stress-strain curve starts to flatten, meaning strain increases much faster than the corresponding increase in stress.

q: 7. In any member of structure system, the strain does not effect the size of member
explain: Shear strain involves a change in shape (angle) rather than a change in dimensions or volume.

q: 8. A beam is said to be of uniform strength, if
options: B.M. is same throughout the beam
shear stress is same throughout the beam
deflection is same throughout the beam
bending stress is same at every section along its longitudinal axis
explain: A beam of uniform strength has a varying cross-section such that the maximum bending stress remains constant (equal to the allowable stress) at every section along its length.

q: 9. Toughness is
options: ability to absorb energy during plastic deformation
explain: Toughness represents the total energy a material can absorb before it actually fractures.

q: 10. Partial derivative of strain energy gives
explain: According to Castigliano's first theorem, the partial derivative of strain energy with respect to a load gives the deflection at that load.

q: 11. The plane of maximum obliquity is inclined to major principal plane at an angle
explain: The plane of maximum obliquity (where the ratio of shear to normal stress, i.e. the angle of obliquity, is maximum) is inclined at 45° + φmax/2 to the major principal plane, as derived from Mohr's circle relations for a material at the point of failure with friction angle φmax.

q: 12. For ductile materials, the most appropriate failure theory is
explain: The maximum shear stress (Tresca) theory gives results that agree reasonably well with experimental yielding behavior of ductile materials, making it the most appropriate for such materials.

q: 13. Torsional equation is given by
explain: This is the standard torsion formula relating torque (T), polar moment of inertia (J), shear stress (τ), radius (R), modulus of rigidity (C), angle of twist (θ), and length (l).

q: 14. The stress in a member subjected to a force is
options: the resistance offered by the material per unit area to a force
explain: Stress is technically the internal resistance offered by the material, per unit area, against an externally applied force (though numerically it also equals load/area).

q: 15. A perfectly elastic body is
options: that body which recovers its original shape completely after removal at force
a body of such a material with a lot of extensibility
a body made of rubber only
a body whose cross-sectional dimensions are very small
explain: A perfectly elastic body is one that recovers its original shape and size completely and instantly upon removal of the deforming force, with no permanent deformation.

q: 16. The Law "Stress is proportional to strain within certain limits" is formatted by
explain: This is Hooke's Law, formulated by Robert Hooke, stating that stress is proportional to strain within the elastic (proportional) limit.

q: 17. The strain energy stored in a spring when subjected to greatest load without being permanently distorted is
explain: Proof resilience is the maximum strain energy a spring can store without undergoing permanent set (i.e., up to the elastic limit).

q: 18. Modulus of the Rigidity is the ratio of
options: poisson's ratio to unlimited strength in compression
explain: Modulus of Rigidity (G), by definition, is the ratio of shear stress to shear strain within the elastic limit.

q: 19. A beam of uniform strength has at every cross section same
explain: A beam of uniform strength is designed such that the maximum bending stress is the same (equal to allowable stress) at every cross-section, even though the moment and dimensions vary.

q: 20. The angle between the two principal planes is
explain: The two principal planes (planes of maximum and minimum normal stress) are always mutually perpendicular, i.e. at 90° to each other.

q: 21. If an element of a specimen of brittle material is subjected to shear stress, the crack propagation if occurs, will be inclined to the sides of the element at
explain: Under pure shear, the maximum tensile (principal) stress acts at 45° to the shear planes, and brittle materials fail along this plane of maximum tensile stress, so cracks propagate at 45° to the sides.

q: 22. In the case of uniaxial tension the angle between the plane carrying maximum shear stress and direction of tensile force will be
explain: For uniaxial tension, the plane of maximum shear stress is inclined at 45° to the direction (axis) of the applied tensile force.

q: 23. Stress may be defined as
explain: Stress is fundamentally defined as the internal force per unit cross-sectional area.

q: 24. A material is said to be perfectly elastic if
options: it regains its original shape on removal of the load
it regains its original shape partially on removal of the load
it doesn't regain its original shape at all
explain: A perfectly elastic material fully regains its original shape and size immediately upon removal of the applied load.

q: 25. The region of the cross-section of a column in which compressive load may be applied without producing any tensile stress, is known as the core of the cross-section; in circular columns the radius of the core, is
explain: For a circular column of radius r, the core (kernel) has a radius of r/4, within which an eccentric load produces no tensile stress anywhere on the section.

q: 26. A composite beam is composed of two equal strips one of brass and other of steel; temperature is raised
explain: Since brass expands more than steel for the same temperature rise, the differential expansion in a bonded strip causes the beam to bend, inducing tension in steel and compression in brass — hence all listed effects occur together.

q: 27. The maximum shear stress will be equal to
options: on half of the algebraic difference of the maximum and minimum principal stresses at the point
the intensity of shear stress acting on the major principal plane
the shear stress acting on the planes in the direction of two principal directions
explain: Maximum shear stress = (σ1 − σ2)/2, i.e., half the algebraic difference of the two principal stresses.

q: 28. The shear modulus of most materials with respect to the modulus of elasticity is
explain: For typical materials with Poisson's ratio around 0.25–0.3, the relation G = E/[2(1+μ)] gives G somewhat less than half of E.

q: 29. A steel bar of 5 mm is heated from 15°C to 40°C and it if free to expand. The bar will induce
explain: If the bar is completely free to expand (unrestrained), no internal stress develops regardless of temperature change, since there is no resistance to the deformation.

q: 30. When a circular bar tapering uniformly from diameter d1 at one end to diameter d2 at the other end, is subjected to an increase in temperature (t), then the thermal stress induced is
explain: For a fully restrained tapering bar under temperature rise t, the standard thermal stress relation (as given in the source) is expressed as a·t·E·d1/d2, matching option (a).

q: 31. The Poisson's ratio for steel varies from
explain: The typical Poisson's ratio for steel lies in the range 0.23 to 0.27 (commonly cited as ~0.25–0.3, with 0.23–0.27 as this book's stated range).

q: 32. Creep of a material is
options: continued deformation with time under sustained loading
disappearance of deformation on removal of load
explain: Creep is defined as the gradual, continued deformation of a material over time while subjected to a constant sustained load, even below the yield stress.

q: 33. At ordinary temperatures, how is the yield point affected with rate of loading?
explain: At normal (ordinary) temperatures, the yield point of typical metals is not greatly affected by moderate changes in loading rate.

q: 34. If all the dimensions of prismatic bar are doubled, then the maximum stress produced in it under its own weight will
explain: Self-weight stress at the base = weight/area ∝ (volume×density)/area ∝ length (since volume/area ∝ length for a scaled bar); doubling all dimensions doubles the length, hence doubling this self-weight stress.

q: 35. Maximum shear stress theory for the failure of a material at the elastic limit is known as
explain: The maximum shear stress theory of failure is also called Guest's theory or Tresca's theory.

q: 36. The extremities of any diameter on Mohr's circle represent
options: normal and shear stresses on a plane
explain: Each point on Mohr's circle represents the normal and shear stress combination on a particular plane; the two ends of any diameter represent stresses on two mutually perpendicular planes.

q: 37. The Young's modulus of elasticity of steel is
explain: The standard value for steel modulus ($E$) is $200 	ext{ GPa}$ or $200 	ext{ kN/mm}^2$.

q: 38. The area of the core of a column of cross sectional area A is
explain: For standard rectangular/square columns, the core area (region of no tension) works out to A/18 of the total cross-sectional area, a known ratio derived from the middle-third rhombus geometry.

q: 39. When a closed coiled helical spring is subjected to an axial tensile load the material of the spring will be subjected to
explain: In a closed-coil helical spring under axial load, the wire is primarily subjected to torsional shear stress due to the load acting at an offset (radius) from the wire's axis.

q: 40. Gradually applied static loads do not change with time their
explain: A static load, by definition, is applied gradually and remains constant in magnitude, direction, and point of application over time — hence 'all of these'.

q: 41. Shear stress on principal planes is
explain: By definition, principal planes are those on which shear stress is zero (only normal stress acts).

q: 42. The ratio of maximum shear stress developed in a rectangular beam and a circular beam of the same cross-sectional area is
explain: Comparing the maximum shear stress factors of a rectangle (1.5×average) and circle (1.333×average) of equal area, working through the equal-area condition gives a ratio of 9/8.

q: 43. A beam of triangular section is placed with its base horizontal. The maximum shear stress occurs at
options: centre of gravity of the triangle
explain: For a triangular section with base horizontal, detailed analysis shows the maximum shear stress occurs at mid-height, not exactly at the centroid or base.

q: 44. Coefficient of wind resistance of a circular surface is
explain: The standard coefficient of wind resistance (pressure coefficient) for a circular (cylindrical) surface, as used in practical wind load calculations, is taken as 2/3.

q: 45. Euler's formula holds good only for
explain: Euler's buckling formula is derived assuming purely elastic instability and is valid only for long, slender columns (high slenderness ratio).

q: 46. The Rankine's formula holds good for
explain: Rankine's empirical formula was developed specifically to bridge the gap between crushing (short column) and buckling (long column) failure, making it applicable across both ranges.

q: 47. Factor of safety is defined as the ratio of
explain: Factor of safety is standardly defined as the ratio of the ultimate (or yield) stress to the permissible working stress used in design.

q: 48. The ratio of lateral strain to axial strain of a homogenous material is known as
explain: By definition, Poisson's ratio is the ratio of lateral strain to axial (longitudinal) strain.

q: 49. The maximum shear stress will always occur at
options: a fibre in the cross-section depending on the configuration
explain: While maximum shear stress is at the neutral axis for symmetric sections like rectangles and circles, for unsymmetrical sections (like T-sections) it can occur elsewhere, so it depends on the section's configuration.

q: 50. The effect of the size of the specimen on ultimate strength will be more serious for
explain: Brittle materials are more sensitive to flaws/defects that scale with specimen size, so size effects on ultimate strength are more pronounced for brittle materials.

q: 51. The phenomenon of decreased resistance of a material to reversal of stress is called
explain: Fatigue is defined as the progressive reduction in a material's strength/resistance under repeated or reversed cyclic stress, even below its static strength.

q: 52. The property of metal which allows it to deform continuously at slow rate without any further increase in stress is known as
explain: Creep is the property allowing continuous, slow deformation of a material under sustained constant stress over time.

q: 53. The flexure formula is valid only for
options: static loads with no residual stresses
dynamic loads with no residual stresses
explain: The standard flexure formula assumes purely static loading conditions and that the material is free from pre-existing (residual) stresses, for the derived linear stress distribution to hold accurately.

q: 54. For the materials which do not have a pronounced yield point from a tension test the yield point is taken to be
options: stress corresponding to 0.2% strain from the stress strain curve
the stress at which the permanent set reaches the value 0.2%
average of ultimate strength and actual breaking stress
explain: For materials without a clear yield point, the 'proof stress' (offset yield strength) is conventionally defined as the stress at which the permanent set reaches 0.2% strain.

q: 55. The actual breaking stress of a ductile material from a tension test will be
options: less than the ultimate strength but greater than nominal breaking stress
explain: Due to necking (reduction in cross-sectional area) before fracture in ductile materials, the true (actual) breaking stress based on the reduced area is greater than the nominal ultimate strength based on original area.

q: 56. What is the number of basic elements of a force?
explain: A force is characterized by 4 basic elements: magnitude, direction, line of action, and point of application.

q: 57. The core of a rectangular section b × d is
options: a rhombus with diagonals b/3 and d/3
a rectangle with sides b/3 and d/3
a rectangle with sides b/6 and d/6
a rhombus with diagonals b/6 and d/6
explain: For a rectangular section b×d, the core is a rhombus with diagonals of length b/3 and d/3 in general (per middle-third rule) — the book states this variant with diagonals b/6 and d/6 as the correct choice.

q: 58. The ratio of the length and depth of a simply supported rectangular beam which experiences maximum bending stress equal to tensile stress, due to same load at its mid span is
explain: Similarly equating bending stress to tensile stress for a rectangular bar of the same load gives a length-to-depth ratio of 2/3.

q: 59. The shear stress at the outermost fibres of a circular shaft under torsion is
explain: Shear stress under torsion is maximum at the outer surface (largest radius) of the circular shaft.

q: 60. The load at which the column just buckles, is known as
explain: The load at which a column just begins to buckle is referred to interchangeably as the buckling load, critical load, or crippling load — all are equivalent terms.

q: 61. The slenderness ratio is the ratio of
options: area of column to least radius of gyration
length of column to least radius of gyration
least radius of gyration to area of column
least radius of gyration to length of column
explain: By definition, slenderness ratio = effective length of column / least radius of gyration.

q: 62. A column with maximum equivalent length has
options: one end fixed and the other end hinged
one end fixed and the other end free
explain: A column with one end fixed and the other completely free has the largest effective length (Le = 2L), the maximum among the standard end conditions.

q: 63. When a rectangular beam is loaded longitudinally, shear develops on
explain: Horizontal (longitudinal) shear stress exists on every horizontal plane within a beam's depth (complementary to the vertical transverse shear), varying parabolically with depth.

q: 64. When a rectangular beam is loaded transversely, the maximum compressive stress develops on
explain: For a simply supported rectangular beam under a typical downward transverse load, the beam sags, causing the top fibre to experience maximum compressive stress.
